slides.heading: Merge Sorted Arrays
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Very Hard · Heaps
slides.narration: Let's solve Merge Sorted Arrays, a very hard heaps problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Merge k sorted lists into one sorted list using a min-heap of (value, list, index).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Merge k sorted lists into one sorted list using a min-heap of (value, list, index).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: A min-heap holds the head of each list; popping it always gives the next smallest overall.
slides.narration: A min-heap holds the head of each list; popping it always gives the next smallest overall.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Concatenate and sort → O(N log N)
Min-heap of k heads → O(N log k)
slides.narration: Concatenating and sorting ignores the existing order. A min-heap holding one element per array always yields the next smallest in log k.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 3. Push the next from that list
slides.narration: Step by step. First, push each list's first element. Second, pop the min and append. Third, push the next from that list. Fourth, repeat.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We seed the heap with each array's first element, then poll, append, and push that array's next element.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n log k. Space is O of n plus k.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
slides.narration: Skip empty arrays when seeding the heap.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
slides.narration: Pairwise divide-and-conquer merging is also N log k.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: A min-heap holds the head of each list; popping it always gives the next smallest overall.
slides.narration: To recap Merge Sorted Arrays: A min-heap holds the head of each list; popping it always gives the next smallest overall. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
